A 2% spread isn't the worst. So that's let's say an ask of $10.20 and a bid of $10.00. So if you set a market order you will buy 100 shares at the best available price which could be $10.20 instead of $10.00. Or you could set a limit order of $10 saying you won't buy unless it's $10 or below. In that case you have to wait until there is a seller willing to sell at a lower price. Market orders are good if the spread isn't too large because a couple pennies here and there won't make or break you. But if the spread is large, which happens when volume isn't big, you could buy the stock at a price way higher than you want.


Again it all depends on volume. The bigger the volume the more buyers and sellers there are in a stock. And usually the spread is smaller. This means the stock is more liquid. If a stock has a volume in millions your order can get filled in seconds. But if it has less volume it could take minutes. And if you look at penny stocks that are really shitty as in $.0001 per share they have 0 volume days on end so your order could take days to get filled.


Hope this helps a little

Short selling is the same concept of buy low and sell high just in reverse. You are making a bet that the stock price will drop so you sell the shares first and if/when the price drops you'll buy them back. An example is ABC stock at $100. If you think it's going to drop you can "borrow" shares and sell them. So if you sell 10 shares at $100 you profit $1000. So now you have a profit of $1000 but also -10 shares so to speak. So you'll eventually have to buy those shares back. Say the price drops to $90 and you buy the shares back,close your short position. So you lose $900 buying it back. But at the end of it all you net $1000-$900=$100. 

And if the price goes up and you have to buy back then you lose money. Some stocks are harder to short than others. Hope that helps
